title: Fluent Is Not the Same as True
paragraphs: Large language models can draft essays, summarise reports and answer questions in fluent prose, which makes it easy to forget how they are built. Most current systems rest on the transformer, an architecture described by researchers at Google in 2017, and are trained on enormous collections of text to predict which word fragment, or token, is likely to come next. Later stages of training, often guided by human feedback, refine its behaviour, but the underlying skill remains statistical prediction.

This design explains both the strengths and the characteristic failures of the technology. Because a model is trained to produce plausible continuations rather than to check claims against the world, it can state an invented citation or a wrong date with the same confidence as a correct one. Developers call these errors hallucinations, and OpenAI's own technical report on GPT-4 acknowledged in 2023 that the model was not fully reliable. The same report noted that the system generally lacked knowledge of events after most of its training data had been collected.

Whether such systems understand anything remains contested. In a widely cited 2021 paper, Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru and colleagues described language models as stochastic parrots, stitching together linguistic forms without reference to meaning. Other researchers counter that the ability to solve unfamiliar problems suggests some internal representation of the world, even if it differs from ours.

For practical purposes, the philosophical debate matters less than a simple discipline. Fluency is evidence that a model has absorbed the patterns of human writing, not evidence that a particular sentence is true. Treating its output as a draft to be verified, rather than as a verdict to be trusted, lets users benefit from the speed without inheriting the errors.
